concepts.title: Balanced and Unbalanced Forces
concepts.explanation:
You can describe motion now - speed, and the shape of a distance/time graph. The next question is what changes it.

An object almost always has several forces on it at once, and what matters is not how many but whether they cancel. Add up the forces on an object, taking direction into account, and what is left over is the RESULTANT force. If the forces cancel exactly the resultant is zero and the forces are balanced. If they do not, the resultant points somewhere and the forces are unbalanced.

The rule is short and is not what most people expect. BALANCED forces do not mean the object is still - they mean its motion does not change. A book on a table is still, and stays still. A lorry on a motorway at a steady 90 km/h also has balanced forces: the engine's drive forward exactly equals the friction and air resistance backward, and because they balance, the speed holds. Nothing is needed to keep it moving; something is needed only to CHANGE how it moves.

UNBALANCED forces change motion. A resultant force forward makes an object speed up; backward, slow down; sideways, change direction. On a distance/time graph that shows as the line bending rather than staying straight.

So a steady speed and standing still are the same case as far as forces are concerned, which is the part worth holding on to. Press the brake in that lorry and the backward forces now exceed the drive: the resultant is backward, the lorry slows, and the graph's line begins to flatten.
concepts.example: A parachutist falls faster and faster at first, because gravity's pull exceeds the air resistance - unbalanced, downward. As she speeds up the air resistance grows until it equals her weight. From that moment the forces are balanced and she falls at a steady speed the rest of the way down, without slowing or speeding up.

concepts.title: Turning Forces, and How to Calculate One
concepts.explanation:
Push a door in the middle and it swings. Push it just beside the hinge, with the same effort, and it hardly moves. The force was the same, so something else decides how much turning you get.

When a force turns something about a fixed point, that point is the PIVOT, and the turning effect is called the MOMENT of the force. It depends on two things: how big the force is, and how far from the pivot it acts. The further out, the more turning for the same push - which is why a door handle is fitted at the edge and never next to the hinges.

It is calculated like this:

    moment = force x perpendicular distance from the pivot

Force in newtons, distance in metres, and the moment comes out in newton metres (Nm). A force of 20 N acting 0.5 m from a pivot gives a moment of 10 Nm. The same 20 N at 1.5 m gives 30 Nm - three times the turning from an identical push.

That is the whole principle behind a lever. A long spanner undoes a tight nut that a short one will not, because the extra length multiplies the moment. A wheelbarrow lets one person lift a load that would be far too heavy to carry, because the load sits close to the wheel - the pivot - while the hands are far from it.

When something balances on a pivot, like a see-saw, the moments turning it one way equal the moments turning it the other. A light child far out can balance a heavy one sitting close in, and now you can work out exactly where.
concepts.example: A 300 N child sits 1.2 m from the middle of a see-saw, giving a moment of 360 Nm. A 450 N child must sit closer to balance it: 360 divided by 450 is 0.8 m. The heavier child has less distance to work with, which is why the small one always ends up out at the end.

concepts.title: Pressure: The Same Force, Spread Differently
concepts.explanation:
Stand on soft ground in flat shoes and you leave a shallow print. Stand on the same ground in one narrow heel and it sinks in. Your weight has not changed. What changed is how much ground it was spread over.

PRESSURE is the force acting on each unit of area:

    pressure = force / area

Force in newtons and area in square metres gives pressure in newtons per square metre, which has its own name: the pascal (Pa). Because area is underneath, the same force gives MORE pressure on a smaller area and LESS on a larger one.

That one relationship explains a great deal of design. A knife is sharpened so its force acts on an almost invisible area, producing pressure high enough to part what it touches - a blunt knife has the same force behind it and too much area to cut with. A drawing pin has a broad head to push on and a fine point to push with, deliberately. Going the other way: a tractor wears wide tyres and a camel has broad feet so their considerable weight is spread and neither sinks, and lying flat is the advice on thin ice because it spreads your weight over the largest area you have.

Liquids and gases press too, and in every direction rather than just down. The pressure in a liquid grows with depth, because there is more liquid above pressing down, which is why a dam is built thick at the bottom and thin at the top, and why a diver feels it in the ears.
concepts.example: A person of weight 600 N stands on two flat soles of total area 0.03 m2, giving 20,000 Pa. The same person balanced on one stiletto heel of area 0.0001 m2 gives 6,000,000 Pa - three hundred times as much, from exactly the same 600 N.

concepts.title: Why a Gas Pushes Back
concepts.explanation:
A football holds its shape because the air inside pushes outward on the skin. Nothing is pushing it deliberately, so where does the push come from? The particle model answers it, and the answer explains everything else a gas does under pressure.

The particles in a gas are spread far apart and moving fast in every direction. Each one that strikes the wall of its container bounces off, and each bounce gives the wall a tiny push. There are so many particles and so many collisions every second that the pushes add up to a steady outward force spread over the whole inside surface. That is gas pressure: the total effect of countless collisions.

Three predictions follow, and all three are testable. Squeeze the gas into a smaller space and the particles hit the walls more often, so the pressure rises - which is why a pumped tyre is hard and why squeezing a sealed syringe gets harder the further you push. Warm the gas and the particles move faster, hit harder and more often, and the pressure rises again - which is why a sealed can must never be heated. Put more gas in and there are simply more particles colliding, which is what a pump does.

Liquid pressure works by the same collisions but with a difference that matters: the particles in a liquid are already touching, so a liquid cannot be squeezed into a smaller space to speak of. That is exactly why hydraulic brakes work - push the fluid at one end and it must move at the other, because there is no give in it.
concepts.example: A sealed syringe with its nozzle blocked can be pushed in some way with effort, and springs back when released - the gas inside was compressed and its pressure rose. Fill the same syringe with water and block it, and it will barely move at all: the particles are already in contact and have nowhere to go.

concepts.title: Diffusion: Substances Mixing Themselves
concepts.explanation:
Someone opens a bottle of perfume at the other side of a still room and a minute later you can smell it. Nobody fanned it towards you and there was no draught. The perfume travelled on its own.

DIFFUSION is the spreading of one substance through another by the ordinary movement of their particles, until the two are evenly mixed. It needs no stirring and no current. The particles of a gas or a liquid are already moving constantly in all directions, and that movement alone carries them into every space available.

It has a direction, and the direction is what makes it useful to know. A substance diffuses from where its particles are CROWDED to where they are sparse - from high concentration to low - because in a crowded region more particles happen to be moving outward than inward. When the crowding has evened out, the particles keep moving but the net flow stops.

It happens in liquids as well as gases, and more slowly, because the particles are packed tighter and get in each other's way: a drop of ink in still water will colour the whole glass eventually. Warming speeds it up, since faster particles spread faster. Solids barely diffuse at all, because their particles only vibrate in place.

Diffusion is how oxygen crosses from the air in your lungs into your blood, and how carbon dioxide crosses back - no pump for that last step, just a difference in crowding and particles that never stop moving.
concepts.example: A crystal of purple potassium permanganate is dropped into a beaker of still water. Nobody stirs it. Over an hour the purple spreads outward from the crystal until the whole beaker is evenly coloured - and it never un-mixes afterwards, because there is nothing to drive the particles back into a crowd.

concepts.title: Inside the Atom
concepts.explanation:
You have used atoms as the smallest piece of an element - the full stop at the end of matter. They are not the end. An atom has parts, and knowing them explains why the Periodic Table is shaped as it is.

Rutherford's experiments early in the twentieth century produced the model still used today. An atom has a tiny central NUCLEUS holding nearly all of its mass, and around that nucleus, in the enormous empty space outside it, move the ELECTRONS. The proportions are hard to credit: if the nucleus were a marble on the centre spot of a football pitch, the nearest electrons would be out beyond the stands. An atom is overwhelmingly empty space.

Three particles matter. PROTONS sit in the nucleus and carry a positive charge. NEUTRONS sit in the nucleus with them and carry no charge at all. ELECTRONS move outside and carry a negative charge, equal in size to the proton's and opposite in sign. An ordinary atom has as many electrons as protons, so the charges cancel exactly and the atom overall is neutral.

What holds it together is the last piece: opposite charges attract. The positive nucleus pulls on the negative electrons, and that ELECTROSTATIC ATTRACTION is what keeps them from flying off. It is the same force that makes a rubbed balloon cling to a wall, acting over a distance far too small to see.

This is why the particle model you used earlier - atoms as small solid spheres - is a useful model and not a picture of the truth. It gets the behaviour of gases and liquids right while being wrong about almost everything inside.
concepts.example: A carbon atom has 6 protons and 6 electrons, so its charges cancel and it is neutral. Take one electron away and the balance is broken: 6 positive and 5 negative leaves an overall charge of +1. Nothing was added; the charge appeared because the cancelling stopped.

concepts.title: Some Metals React Hard, and Some Hardly At All
concepts.explanation:
Gold rings survive centuries. Iron nails rust in a season. A small piece of potassium dropped in water skitters about and catches fire. All three are metals, and they could hardly behave less alike.

Metals can be put in order of how vigorously they react, and that order is called the REACTIVITY SERIES. From most reactive to least: potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, zinc, iron, copper, silver, gold. It is worth learning, because the same order predicts three different sets of reactions.

With WATER: potassium and sodium react violently, fizzing and skidding, and potassium's hydrogen catches fire. Calcium fizzes steadily. Magnesium reacts only very slowly with cold water. Zinc and iron do not react with cold water at all - iron needs water AND air together, which is what rusting is. Copper, silver and gold do nothing whatever.

With OXYGEN: the reactive metals tarnish within moments of being cut, which is why sodium is kept under oil. Magnesium burns with a fierce white light. Iron burns only as fine wool or filings. Gold does not tarnish at all, which is why it is still bright after a thousand years in the ground.

With DILUTE ACIDS: everything above copper fizzes, giving off hydrogen, faster the higher up the series. Copper, silver and gold give no reaction.

So the series is not three facts but one, and the reason we can have iron water pipes and gold jewellery and must keep potassium under oil.

Copper, silver and gold sit at the bottom of the series for the same reason across all three tests: they resist reacting almost completely. Chemists have a word for a substance that behaves like that - they call it INERT. Gold is the clearest example among the metals, but it is not the only kind: the noble gases, the elements in the Periodic Table's final group, are inert too, which is why a party balloon can be filled with helium and last for days without the gas reacting with anything inside or outside it. Inert does not mean 'never reacts under any circumstances' - it means 'so unreactive that, for ordinary purposes, it might as well not react at all'.
concepts.example: Equal pieces of magnesium, zinc and copper are dropped into the same dilute acid. The magnesium fizzes hard and disappears within a minute; the zinc fizzes gently and takes much longer; the copper sits there unchanged for as long as you care to watch. That is the reactivity series, visible in one experiment.

concepts.title: Writing a Reaction Down
concepts.explanation:
Describing a reaction in a sentence takes a long time and is easy to get vague about. Chemists write it as a WORD EQUATION instead, and the form carries information that a sentence tends to lose.

The reactants - the substances you start with - go on the left. The products - the new substances made - go on the right. An arrow between them means 'becomes', and it points one way, because a reaction has a direction. A plus sign separates two substances on the same side.

    magnesium + oxygen -> magnesium oxide

Read it aloud as "magnesium reacts with oxygen to make magnesium oxide". Three things are now fixed that a sentence might have left loose: exactly what went in, exactly what came out, and which was which.

The arrow is not an equals sign and the two sides are not interchangeable. Writing magnesium oxide on the left would describe a completely different process. Reversing an equation makes a claim about a reaction that may not happen at all.

Some more, worth being able to read:

    zinc + hydrochloric acid -> zinc chloride + hydrogen
    calcium carbonate -> calcium oxide + carbon dioxide
    glucose + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water

Notice that the second has one reactant and two products: a single substance broken apart by heating. Nothing says the number of substances must match across the arrow. What must match is the atoms - none appears from nowhere and none vanishes - which is why the name of every element on the left turns up somewhere on the right.
concepts.example: Iron rusting, written out: iron + oxygen + water -> hydrated iron oxide. The equation makes plain what a sentence often blurs - that rusting needs all THREE reactants, which is why a nail in dry air and a nail in boiled sealed water both stay bright.

concepts.title: Reactions That Warm, and Reactions That Cool
concepts.explanation:
Touch the outside of a beaker during a reaction and you learn something the reaction does not otherwise show: every chemical change moves energy, and it goes one of two ways.

An EXOTHERMIC reaction releases energy to its surroundings, mostly as heat, so the mixture and its container get warmer. Burning is the obvious case - that is the whole point of a fire - but so is a metal reacting with an acid, and so is the setting of cement. Respiration in your own cells is exothermic, which is a large part of why you are warm.

An ENDOTHERMIC reaction takes energy IN from its surroundings, so the mixture gets colder. These surprise people, because a reaction that cools things sounds like it is running backwards. Dissolve ammonium nitrate in water and the beaker becomes cold enough to be uncomfortable to hold; that is the principle of an instant cold pack for a sports injury. Photosynthesis is endothermic, taking in the energy of sunlight. So is thermal decomposition: heating calcium carbonate only works while the heat keeps coming, because the reaction is swallowing it.

The test is simply a thermometer in the mixture, before and during. A rise means exothermic, a fall endothermic, and the size of the change says how much energy moved.

It is worth being careful about one thing. 'Endothermic' does not mean a reaction that needs heating to get started - plenty of exothermic reactions need a match. It means the reaction takes energy in overall while it runs. A bonfire needs lighting and then gives out far more than it took.
concepts.example: Two beakers, each with a thermometer. Magnesium is added to acid in the first and the reading climbs from 21 to 34 degrees - exothermic. Ammonium nitrate is stirred into water in the second and the reading falls from 21 to 8 degrees - endothermic, and the outside of the beaker mists over.

concepts.title: Why What Comes Out Is Rarely Pure
concepts.explanation:
A word equation is tidy: reactants in, products out. Real reactions are less obliging, and knowing why is what separates a chemist from someone who has only read the equation.

A PURE substance is one single substance and nothing else. It has sharp fixed melting and boiling points, which is how purity is tested: pure water freezes at exactly 0 degrees and boils at exactly 100 at sea level, while anything dissolved in it shifts both and spreads them over a range.

Reactions rarely give you that, for several ordinary reasons. Often more than one product forms at once - burning a fuel in plenty of air gives carbon dioxide, and in poor air gives some carbon monoxide and soot as well, from the same fuel. Often some reactant is left over, because the amounts were not matched exactly, and it stays mixed in with the product. And the reactants themselves were rarely pure to begin with, so whatever came in with them is still there at the end.

So what you have after a reaction is usually a mixture: the product you wanted, some you did not, and leftovers. That is why the separating methods in this unit matter so much - filtering, evaporating, distilling and chromatography exist because the interesting substance nearly always has to be got out of a mixture afterwards.

It is also why industry measures purity as a number rather than a yes or no. A medicine at 99.9% pure and one at 95% are both impure, and only one of them is safe to take.
concepts.example: A sample claimed to be pure water is put in a freezer with a thermometer. It begins to freeze at minus 2 degrees and is not fully solid until minus 5 - a range, not a point. It is not pure: something is dissolved in it, and the thermometer found out without anything being separated.

concepts.title: Respiration: Getting the Energy Out of Food
concepts.explanation:
This unit has followed food into the body and shown how it is broken down and absorbed. One question is left, and it is the one all of it was for: how does the food actually become the energy you run on?

The answer is a chemical reaction called AEROBIC RESPIRATION, and it happens in every living cell, every moment of your life. Glucose from your food and oxygen from your lungs react together, releasing the energy stored in the glucose and leaving carbon dioxide and water as waste:

    glucose + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water (+ energy released)

That equation is worth knowing by heart, because it ties together nearly everything in this course. It explains why you must eat - glucose. Why you must breathe in - oxygen. Why you breathe out carbon dioxide - it is the waste. Why you are warm - the reaction is exothermic. And why your heart and lungs work harder when you run: the muscles are respiring faster, so they need glucose and oxygen delivered faster and the carbon dioxide taken away faster.

It happens in a particular place. Inside almost every cell are tiny structures called MITOCHONDRIA, and aerobic respiration takes place inside them. Cells that need a great deal of energy are packed with them: a muscle cell has thousands, where a fat-storage cell has very few. That is not decoration - it is the cell's energy supply, sized to the job.

'Aerobic' means 'with oxygen', which implies there is another kind. There is, and muscles fall back on it briefly when they cannot get oxygen fast enough; it releases far less energy from the same glucose, which is why a sprint cannot be kept up.

One distinction is worth being exact about, because it is easy to blur: BREATHING and RESPIRATION are not two words for the same thing. Breathing, also called ventilation, is the physical, mechanical act of moving air into and out of your lungs. Respiration is the chemical reaction above, happening inside your cells, that breathing exists to supply. Stop breathing and your cells run out of oxygen within minutes; stop respiring and no amount of breathing will save you, because respiration is what the oxygen was for.

Breathing itself is driven by two sets of muscles working together. The DIAPHRAGM is a dome-shaped sheet of muscle stretched beneath your lungs, separating your chest from your abdomen. When it contracts, it flattens and pulls downward, making more space inside your chest. At the same time, the INTERCOSTAL MUSCLES between your ribs contract and pull your rib cage up and outward. Both movements enlarge your chest at once, air rushes in to fill the extra space, and you have inhaled. Relax both sets of muscles and your chest springs back to its resting size, pushing air back out, and you have exhaled. Put a hand flat on your ribs and breathe in deeply, and you can feel your intercostal muscles doing exactly this.
concepts.example: Breathe out through a straw into limewater and it turns cloudy - the carbon dioxide on the right-hand side of the equation, coming from cells all over your body. Do twenty star jumps and repeat: the limewater goes cloudy far faster, because respiration has sped up to supply the energy the muscles just demanded.
